raw_case_text:
Our second case is a 48-year-old Saudi gentleman, a known case of bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, and type II diabetes mellitus on metformin. He is a non-smoker. In February 2018, he presented with a dry cough and progressive dyspnea over 5 days. Later on, he developed dyspnea at rest. He was also complaining of nasal congestion and otalgia. He denied fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis nor did he have skin rash, joint pain, or swelling. Other systematic review was unremarkable. He underwent bilateral tymanectomy due to partial deafness. He underwent colonoscopy twice - the last one in 2017, for recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhea and was diagnosed with eosinophilic colitis.
A general physical examination showed an obese man. His vital signs were as follows: BP 140/70 mmHg, PR 120 beats/minute, RR 32 breaths/minute, T 36.9  C and SpO2 of 89% while breathing ambient air (95% with 2 L' oxygen via nasal cannula). Cardiac examination: neck veins were not distended with normal, accentuated heart sounds. No audible murmurs. Chest auscultation showed bilateral, equal air entry with vesicular breath sounds, and bibasilar, early fine inspiratory rales. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
His CBC showed hemoglobin of 16.8 g/L, WBC count was 15.6 x 109/L and eosinophils were 42% (6552 cells/muL). C-reactive protein was 80 mg/L. His ABG showed PaO2 of 58 mmHg and oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Liver function tests and urine analysis were normal. Serum creatinine was 150 mmol/L. His serum Immunoglobulin E (IgE) was 260 IU/Ml and Aspergillus fumigatus Immunoglobulin E (IgE) was negative. Chest x-ray was normal (Fig. 6). CT chest showed multifocal, micronodular, and acino-alveolar opacities primarily raising the possibility of an infectious process likely spread by bronchogenic and hematogenous routes (Fig. 7, Fig. 8).
He was admitted as a case of asthma exacerbation with possible community-acquired pneumonia. Empirical antimicrobials were initiated along with oxygen therapy, intravenous corticosteroids, nebulized bronchodilators, and intravenous fluids. Abdominal CT was suggestive of mesenteric panniculitis with lymphadenopathy in the central, proximal root of the mesentery and also showed right colon pneumatosis coli with few foci of pneumoretroperitoneum. Subsequent investigations were negative for ANAs and ANCA. Nerve conduction tests showed no neuropathy.
He was diagnosed as CEP in a similar fashion as the first case but he didn't undergo BAL. He was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and discharged 4 days later on oral corticosteroids. The steroid dose was tapered to 5 mg daily over one month. He was receiving inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-agonist (ICS/LABA), long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), and montelukast. The trial to withdraw oral corticosteroids failed and he suffered from weight gain, depression as well as uncontrolled diabetes.
In September 2020, subcutaneous mepolizumab, 100 mg, monthly was started and the oral corticosteroids were stopped successfully. He remained asymptomatic till his follow-up in March 2021. His examination was unremarkable other than expiratory rhonchi without crackles. Follow-up investigations showed a normal chest x-ray (Fig. 9) and CT chest with a drop in eosinophil count to 5% (270 cells/muL). His current medications are ICS/LABA, LAMA, montelukast, and monthly mepolizumab. His FEV1 was 60% pre-therapy and 72% after therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old non-smoking Saudi man with bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eosinophilic colitis presented with a 5-day history of dry cough and progressive dyspnea at rest accompanied by nasal congestion and otalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In February 2018, the patient developed a dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnea over 5 days that worsened to dyspnea at rest, accompanied by nasal congestion and ear pain. Although he responded rapidly to high-dose glucocorticoids for chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, attempts to withdraw oral corticosteroids failed and resulted in weight gain, depression, and uncontrolled diabetes until monthly subcutaneous mepolizumab was initiated in September 2020.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin, biopsy-proven eosinophilic colitis (diagnosed on colonoscopy in 2017 for recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhea), and partial deafness status post bilateral tympanectomy; lifetime non-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, dyspnea at rest, nasal congestion, and otalgia; negative for fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, skin rash, or arthralgias/arthritis.

objective.physical_examination: Obese male; admission vitals: BP 140/70 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, temperature 36.9 C, and room-air SpO2 89% (95% on 2 L/min nasal cannula). Chest auscultation revealed bilateral equal vesicular breath sounds with bibasilar early fine inspiratory crackles; cardiac and systemic exams were otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed hemoglobin 16.8 g/dL, leukocytosis (WBC 15.6 x 10^9/L) with marked peripheral eosinophilia (42%, 6,552 cells/uL; dropping to 5% [270 cells/uL] after mepolizumab), CRP 80 mg/L, room-air PaO2 58 mmHg (SaO2 87%), serum creatinine 150 umol/L, normal LFTs and urinalysis, elevated total serum IgE (260 IU/mL), and negative ANA and ANCA. Nerve conduction studies showed no peripheral neuropathy. Chest X-ray was normal. Pre-mepolizumab FEV1 was 60% predicted (improving to 72% predicted post-mepolizumab).
objective.advanced_workup: Serum Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE was negative. Chest CT demonstrated multifocal micronodular and acino-alveolar opacities (which resolved completely on follow-up chest CT after mepolizumab). Abdominal CT incidentally showed central mesenteric panniculitis with proximal mesenteric lymphadenopathy and benign right colon pneumatosis coli with trace pneumoretroperitoneum.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Steroid-dependent chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP) in a patient with asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eosinophilic colitis (with incidental mesenteric panniculitis and pneumatosis coli); allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) were excluded by negative Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE, negative ANCA, and normal nerve conduction studies. Initially treated with high-dose IV and oral corticosteroids alongside ICS/LABA, LAMA, and montelukast; following steroid-withdrawal relapses and steroid toxicity (weight gain, depression, uncontrolled diabetes), initiation of monthly subcutaneous mepolizumab (100 mg/month in September 2020) enabled complete discontinuation of oral corticosteroids, sustained symptom remission, FEV1 improvement from 60% to 72%, eosinophil reduction to 270 cells/uL (5%), and complete chest CT resolution at March 2021 follow-up.
